title: Trump's Ex-Lawyer Grilled: Can He Lead Justice Impartially?
summary: Picture this: your former defense lawyer is now in charge of prosecuting everyone—including you. That's the uneasy reality senators confronted on Wednesday, July 15, 2026, as Todd Blanche, President Trump's one-time personal attorney, sat before the Senate Judiciary Committee seeking confirmation as the nation's Attorney General. The hearing crackled with tension over a fundamental question: can the man who defended Trump against 34 felony counts of falsifying business records now impartially lead the Department of Justice? Blanche, 51, didn't shy from his past. "I'm exceedingly grateful" for Trump's support, he said in his opening statement. But he quickly pivoted to safer ground, touting a drop in violent crime in 2025 and DOJ efforts against cartels. "None of this is a Republican or Democrat issue," he insisted. Yet his actions as acting AG tell a more complicated story. In May, Blanche oversaw a civil settlement that effectively shielded Trump and his family from future IRS tax investigations—a move critics call a glaring conflict of interest. He has also pursued prosecutions of Trump's perceived enemies, including former FBI Director James Comey. Democrats on the panel pressed hard on whether the DOJ is being "weaponized"—a term Blanche himself used to describe the department's pre-Trump actions. "In recent years, we watched the Justice Department turned against many of you and a former president," Blanche said, echoing Trump's grievances. "We are fixing that." Republicans largely defended him, arguing he's restoring trust. But legal scholars note that even without confirmation, Trump could keep Blanche in an acting role indefinitely. The hearing, set to continue Thursday, is widely seen as a referendum on the DOJ's independence under Trump. With the Senate narrowly divided, Blanche's confirmation is on a knife's edge. The outcome could redefine the boundary between law and loyalty for years to come.
why_it_matters: Whether the person leading the Justice Department is independent or loyal to one person affects the rule of law — the idea that everyone must follow the same rules. This confirmation fight could set a precedent for how politics and justice mix, influencing whether young people grow up in a country where the legal system is truly fair and impartial.

background_read: The Attorney General is the head of the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ), the federal agency that enforces laws and represents the country in legal matters.
Nominees must be approved by the Senate Judiciary Committee, a panel that holds hearings to examine qualifications and potential conflicts of interest.

Todd Blanche was previously a federal prosecutor before becoming a defense attorney; he gained national attention defending Trump in a New York trial for 34 felony counts of falsifying business records — a crime involving secret hush-money payments.

The DOJ traditionally operates with a degree of independence from the White House to avoid political influence over investigations; Trump’s first term saw clashes with former FBI Director James Comey, whom he fired.
Trump’s conflict with Comey and other justice officials led to ongoing debates about the ‘weaponization’ of law enforcement for political purposes.

perspectives.description: Supporters contend that Blanche’s insider knowledge and experience prosecuting cartels could make the DOJ more effective at fighting violent crime and restoring order.
Opponents fear that putting Trump’s personal lawyer at the helm erodes the DOJ’s independence, turning it into a shield for the president’s allies and a sword against his critics.

The debate over Blanche’s confirmation is the latest in a years-long struggle to define the boundary between the White House and federal law enforcement — a boundary that has grown increasingly blurred regardless of which party holds power.

If Blanche is confirmed or remains acting AG, future administrations may face pressure to pass laws limiting the president’s ability to install personal attorneys in top justice roles, setting a new standard for DOJ independence.
